reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in educational services, NAICS 61, at 30.0% of firms in the latest period, down from 35.5% in the prior period. The question asked is whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and the survey first asked it in September 2023. That is the only measured adoption figure in this material, and it describes firms answering for themselves, not students, faculty, or institutions as a whole.

The Department of Education issued the federal guidance, and its page carries an inventory of the Department's own AI use-cases, which is the clearest picture here of what education-adjacent organizations actually deploy AI for. The listed uses include CAISY, described as delivering real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation to streamline repetitive tasks and improve situational awareness, Grammarly's AI assistant for written communication, Otter.AI for real-time transcription and collaboration, and AWS Bedrock for building applications on foundation models. Other entries cover generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in multiple programming languages, writing R code for data analysis, training employees in prompt engineering, converting data types such as a county name into its FIPS code, generating mock datasets for testing, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, extracting action items from public articles and policies, testing filters with fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information, and drafting descriptive paragraphs, workflow diagrams, and qualifications for public positions.

The same Department of Education page sets the regulatory posture. Its OCIO supports the Department's adherence to federal regulations on AI advancement and responsible and secure usage, in accordance with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. The guidance is framed around permissible use, risk, and procurement for US education, which is the compliance backdrop a school or institution is working against rather than a set of performance claims.

HolonIQ tracks the education economy as a market-intelligence platform for the global impact economy, covering EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning. Its page describes sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, scoring impact, and mapping partnerships and competitive landscapes for governments, institutions, technology companies, and investors. It does not, in this material, publish a specific education AI market size or growth rate, so nothing here should be read as one.

Courses and certifications are catalogued here, and that catalog lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, each with a verified source and re-verified daily. The page notes that four are university graduate courses, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, including DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and Andrej Karpathy, and it draws a distinction between exam-driven theory and code-first, hands-on instruction. It also states plainly that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a narrow set of conclusions. Adoption among educational services firms is measured by the Census Bureau at 30.0%, the federal government has published both a use-case inventory and a risk and procurement posture through the Department of Education, and the recurring uses in that inventory are drafting, summarization, transcription, code assistance, and internal analysis rather than instruction itself. The sources here report no ROI figures, no cost savings, and no outcome evidence for education specifically, and HolonIQ's page describes its methods without giving education numbers. The honest reading is that the deployment case rests on documented use patterns and federal guidance, not on measured returns.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
